newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judicial group rejects 12-member jury proposal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judicial group rejects 12-member jury proposal.

text.p: A judicial group that sets policy for the federal court system rejected Tuesday a proposal that would have required the empaneling of a 12-member jury in all civil cases.

The Judicial Conference of the United States, a 27-judge group chaired by Supreme Court Chief Justice William Rehnquist, turned down by voice vote the proposal to amend the federal rules of civil procedures regarding jury size.
But the group agreed to have a committee study the issue further.

U.S. appeals court judge Gilbert Merritt, a member of the group, told a news briefing that opponents of the proposal argued that judges during the past 20 years have experimented with six-member and eight-member juries in some civil cases without any problems.
He said the opponents pointed out smaller juries tend to cost less, are more manageable and generally have the support of federal district court judges.
In other action, the group voted to ask Congress for an additional 21 permanent and 12 temporary district court judgeships to handle the growing number of cases.
